title: GLUCOPHAGE (metformin hydrochloride) tablets and GLUCOPHAGE XR extended-release tablets: full prescribing information
journal: US Food and Drug Administration, Drugs@FDA, NDA 020357 and NDA 021202, label revised May 2018
result: Indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycaemic control in adults and, for the immediate-release tablet, children of 10 years and older with type 2 diabetes. Mechanism of action: decreases hepatic glucose production, decreases intestinal absorption of glucose and improves insulin sensitivity by increasing peripheral glucose uptake and utilisation; insulin secretion remains unchanged. Pharmacokinetics: absolute bioavailability of a 500 mg tablet under fasting conditions about 50 to 60%; steady-state plasma concentrations generally below 1 µg/mL; apparent volume of distribution 654 ± 358 L after 850 mg; negligible plasma protein binding; excreted unchanged in urine with no hepatic metabolism, no identified human metabolites and no biliary excretion; about 90% of absorbed drug eliminated renally within 24 hours; plasma elimination half-life about 6.2 hours and blood half-life about 17.6 hours; renal clearance about 3.5 times creatinine clearance, so tubular secretion is the major route. Single 850 mg dose: peak concentration 1.86 ± 0.52 µg/mL and renal clearance 384 ± 122 mL/min with creatinine clearance 61 to 90 mL/min, against 4.12 ± 1.83 µg/mL and 108 ± 57 mL/min at 31 to 60 mL/min and 3.93 ± 0.92 µg/mL and 130 ± 90 mL/min at 10 to 30 mL/min. Contraindicated at eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2; initiation not recommended at 30 to 45; benefit and risk assessed if eGFR falls below 45; discontinue below 30. Discontinue at or before iodinated contrast imaging when eGFR is 30 to 60 mL/min/1.73 m2, in liver disease, alcoholism or heart failure, or with intra-arterial contrast, and re-evaluate eGFR after 48 hours. Boxed warning: postmarketing metformin-associated lactic acidosis, characterised by blood lactate above 5 mmol/L, anion gap acidosis without ketonuria or ketonaemia, raised lactate to pyruvate ratio and plasma metformin generally above 5 µg/mL; metformin decreases liver uptake of lactate, raising blood lactate; prompt haemodialysis recommended, metformin being dialysable with a clearance up to 170 mL/min. Lactic acidosis reported in about 32% of overdose cases. Vitamin B12: in 29-week trials a decrease to subnormal levels of previously normal serum vitamin B12 occurred in about 7% of patients, possibly through interference with B12 absorption from the B12-intrinsic factor complex, may be associated with anaemia, and appears rapidly reversible on discontinuation or B12 supplementation; measure haematological parameters annually and B12 every 2 to 3 years. Drug interactions: inhibitors of organic cation transporter 2 (OCT2) and multidrug and toxin extrusion (MATE), among them ranolazine, vandetanib, dolutegravir and cimetidine, may increase systemic exposure; single-dose cimetidine 400 mg with metformin 850 mg gave geometric mean ratios of 1.40 for AUC and 1.61 for peak concentration; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as topiramate may increase the risk of lactic acidosis. No clinical study has established conclusive evidence of macrovascular risk reduction. In a 29-week double-blind placebo-controlled US trial in obese patients with type 2 diabetes, fasting plasma glucose changed by −53.0 mg/dL with metformin up to 2550 mg daily (n = 141) and +6.3 mg/dL with placebo (n = 145), and HbA1c by −1.4% and +0.4% (both P = 0.001); mean weight change was −1.4 lb and −2.4 lb. Adverse reactions with metformin against placebo: diarrhoea 53% against 12%, nausea or vomiting 26% against 8%, flatulence 12% against 6%; diarrhoea led to discontinuation in 6%.
